content: Here is the plan for your animation. Generate makes it.

proposal.title: Gradient descent on a quadratic bowl
proposal.description: A bowl-shaped surface shows the loss L = ½(x² + c·y²), with contour lines and its lowest point marked at the centre. A ball sits on the surface at a starting point. Each gradient step moves the ball against the slope, by the learning rate times the gradient, and leaves a trail. An arrow at the ball points in the downhill direction (the negative gradient), which is the direction of the next step. With a small learning rate the ball creeps toward the bottom. In a narrow bowl it zig-zags across the valley, and with too large a learning rate it bounces outward and the loss grows.

input.request: minimize a quadratic loss with gradient steps

interactions: Press play to let the host take gradient steps one after another, or step once at a time.
Use the Take one step action to apply one gradient step and see the ball, trail and readouts update.
Drag the start marker across the bowl to choose where the descent begins.
Use the Restart from start point action to clear the trail and step count while keeping your current settings and start point.
Change the learning rate: small values give many short steps, values near 2/c make the ball zig-zag across the valley, and values above 2/c make it bounce outward.
Change the steepness across the valley: c = 1 gives a round bowl with a straight path to the bottom, and larger values give a long narrow valley.

proposal.original_request: minimize a quadratic loss with gradient steps
proposal.prompt: A bowl-shaped surface shows the loss L = ½(x² + c·y²), with contour lines and its lowest point marked at the centre. A ball sits on the surface at a starting point. Each gradient step moves the ball against the slope, by the learning rate times the gradient, and leaves a trail. An arrow at the ball points in the downhill direction (the negative gradient), which is the direction of the next step. With a small learning rate the ball creeps toward the bottom. In a narrow bowl it zig-zags across the valley, and with too large a learning rate it bounces outward and the loss grows.
requirements: Recommended: experiment. Changing the learning rate and the shape of the bowl, then watching the trail and the loss readout, shows directly why step size matters and when gradient steps settle, zig-zag or blow up.
Interaction: Press play to let the host take gradient steps one after another, or step once at a time.
Interaction: Use the Take one step action to apply one gradient step and see the ball, trail and readouts update.
Interaction: Drag the start marker across the bowl to choose where the descent begins.
Interaction: Use the Restart from start point action to clear the trail and step count while keeping your current settings and start point.
Interaction: Change the learning rate: small values give many short steps, values near 2/c make the ball zig-zag across the valley, and values above 2/c make it bounce outward.
Interaction: Change the steepness across the valley: c = 1 gives a round bowl with a straight path to the bottom, and larger values give a long narrow valley.
Parameter: Learning rate (step size), 0.01 to 0.6, default 0.15
Parameter: Steepness across the valley (c), 1 to 10, default 4

Goal: See that gradient descent moves against the slope, that the learning rate controls whether it converges smoothly, zig-zags or diverges, and that a narrow valley (large c) forces a smaller safe step.
assumptions: This is an illustration: a made-up two-variable quadratic loss, not a trained model on real data.
The loss is L(x, y) = ½(x² + c·y²), so its gradient is (x, c·y) and its minimum is exactly at (0, 0).
Each step is plain gradient descent: new position = old position − learning rate × gradient. There is no momentum or noise, so the path is exactly determined.

Along each axis the position is multiplied by (1 − learning rate) or (1 − learning rate × c) at every step. Steps settle toward the minimum when both factors are between −1 and 1, which means a learning rate below 2/c (and below 2).
The surface's height is drawn vertically compressed so the bowl stays readable at c = 10. The readouts show the true loss values.
Readouts: step count, current loss, gradient size, and the current position (x, y).
limitations: A run stops after 60 steps, or earlier when the ball reaches the edge of the drawn surface (x or y beyond ±3), so the ball stays on the surface. A diverging run is shown by its outward bounce and growing loss up to that point.
Only a quadratic bowl is shown. Real losses are rarely this simple, and on them the safe step size changes from place to place.
With a learning rate between 1/c and 2/c, the loss still falls but the path overshoots the valley floor at every step, so the ball zig-zags rather than moving straight down.
